# Chapter 0 – Learning the basics of R & Python

In this chapter we introduce two of the most widely used programming languages for statistical analysis—R and Python.
Each has unique strengths: R offers a rich ecosystem of statistics-first packages (think ggplot2, dplyr, survival),
whereas Python shines for general-purpose data science and machine-learning pipelines (pandas, scikit-learn, TensorFlow).
Mastering both gives you the flexibility to jump between academic research workflows and industry data-science stacks.

We will not discuse the instalation of the required toolchains since there is a lot of good resources to learn this process
so we star with a walk through their basic syntax, data structures, and plotting libraries. Throughout the chapter you will
see side-by-side code snippets, allowing you to translate a task from one language to the other with minimal friction.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to

- Recognize and use basic data types and data structures

- Perform basic operations and import packages

- Perform exploratory analisys of data

- Ploting insights

Mastering these building blocks will prepare you for the next chapters, where we apply R and Python to more advanced
topics such as hypothesis testing, regression modelling, and simulation.


## Getting Started with R and Python
The first step in mastering any programming language is becoming familiar with its syntax—the set of rules that lets you communicate with a computer.
In practice, your code is passed to an interpreter or compiler that translates those human-readable instructions into machine language the hardware can execute.

### Data types.
Understanding data types is essential because it defines what kind of operations you can perform on a variable.
Mismatched types—like trying to add text to a number—often cause errors or unexpected results.

>**Tip:** Understanding data types is key to avoiding unexpected results.  
>Always check the type of your variables before performing operations on them.

Before writing any analysis, it’s essential to know the basic **data types** that both R and Python offer.  
In the next code block you’ll see how to **create variables**, **inspect their type**, and **compare the syntax** side by side.

::: {.callout-note title="Example: Data types"}
#### Data types
::: {.panel-tabset}
### R
```{r}
#| label: data_types_r
#| code-fold: true      # ← esto crea el botón “Código”
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 4
#| message: false
#| warning: false
integer  <- 2L         # L → integer (32-bit)
typeof(integer)        #> integer

double   <- 3.45
typeof(double)         #> double

string   <- "text"
typeof(string)         #> character

logical  <- TRUE
typeof(logical)        #> logical

complex  <- 1 + 2i
typeof(complex)        #> complex

```
### Python
```{python}
#| label: data_types-py
#| code-fold: true      # ← botón “Código”
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 4
integer  = 2
print(type(integer))    # <class 'int'>

double   = 3.45
print(type(double))     # <class 'float'>

string   = "text"
print(type(string))     # <class 'str'>

boolean  = True
print(type(boolean))    # <class 'bool'>

complex_ = 1 + 2j
print(type(complex_))   # <class 'complex'>

```

:::
:::

**Why do data types matter?**

Every operation you perform on a variable depends on its type. For example, you can’t directly add a character string to a floating-point number because they belong to different data categories. Before combining them, you must convert one type into the other (e.g., cast the number to a string or parse the string as a number). Understanding these constraints—and how each language handles type conversion—prevents bugs and makes your code more readable.

::: {.callout-warning title="Erro: Data types"}
#### Data types error
::: {.panel-tabset}
### R
```{r}
#| label: common error dtype r

#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 4
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| error: true


"5" + 3      # non-numeric argument to binary operator
```

:::
:::

Now that you know the basic types, let's move on to the structures that group them: vectors in R and lists/tuples in Python.

### Data structures.
Data structures determine how information is stored and accessed in memory.
R is built around vectors as its fundamental data structure, while Python's base structures are lists and dictionaries.
Choosing the right structure makes your code more efficient and easier to read.

>**Tip:** Choose the data structure that best fits your task—vectors and lists in R, or lists and dictionaries in Python.  
>Using the right structure will make your code simpler and faster.

Data structures allow us to group and organize multiple elements.  In this section we will see how to create and manipulate the most common collections in R and Python, comparing syntax and behaviors.

::: {.callout-note title="Data structures"}
#### Data structures
::: {.panel-tabset}
### R
```{r}
#| label: ds-r
#| code-fold: true

# Numeric vector
v <- c(1, 2, 3, 4)
print(v)

# Lists
lst <- list(1, "a", TRUE)
print(lst)

# Data frame
df <- data.frame(id = 1:3, name = c("Alice", "Bob", "Carol"))
print(df)
str(df)
```
### Python
```{python}
#| label: ds-py
#| code-fold: true

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

# list
v = [1, 2, 3, 4]
print(v)

# Tuple
t = (1, 2, 3)
print(t)

# Dictionary
d = {"a": 1, "b": 2}
print(d)

# Data frame
df = pd.DataFrame({"id": [1,2,3], "name": ["Alice", "Bob", "Carol"]})
print(df)
df.info()
```

:::
:::

#### Indexing
One of the most important differences between these two languages is how they number positions in a sequence. In R, vectors are 1-based, so the first element is at index 1. In Python, lists (and other sequences) are 0-based, so the first element is at index 0.

::: {.callout-note title="Indexing"}
#### Indexing in R & Python
::: {.panel-tabset}
### R
```{r}
#| label: index-R
#| code-fold: true

v <- c("a", "b", "c")
print(v[1])   # "a"
```
### Python
```{python}
#| label: index-py
#| code-fold: true

v = ["a", "b", "c"]
print(v[0])   # "a"
```
:::
:::
>**Tip:** Remember that R indexes start at 1, while Python indexes start at 0.  
>This difference can cause off-by-one errors if you switch between languages.

### Importing packages
Packages extend the functionality of your base language. Some add entirely new capabilities, while others improve on built-in functions.
Organizing all your package imports at the top of your script makes dependencies clear and avoids runtime surprises.

>**Tip:** Keep your package imports organized at the top of your script.  
>This makes it easier to see dependencies and avoids surprises when running the code later.

Before diving deeper into using R to solve statistical problems of any kind, its essential to understand how to extend the functionality of your programming enviroment. Both R an Python rely on external packages. Collections of functions and tools developed by the community to perform specialized tasks. in this section we'll walk you through how to install and manage packages in both languages so you can confidently access the tools needed for any analysis you aim to perform.

::: {.callout-note title="Importing packages"}
#### Installing packages in R & Python
::: {.panel-tabset}
### R
```{r}
#| label: packages-R
#| code-fold: true

```

:::

### Reading and Writing Data
The ability to read from and write to files allows you to work with real-world datasets stored in formats like CSV and Excel.
Choosing between formats often depends on compatibility, size, and ease of sharing—CSV is lightweight and widely supported, while Excel supports multiple sheets and formatting.

Once you know how to load packages, the next essential skill is reading and writing data files.
In most cases, datasets are stored in formats such as **CSV**, **Excel**, or **TXT**.  
R and Python each provide multiple functions to accomplish this; here we focus on the most common and beginner-friendly options.

::: {.callout-note title="Example: Reading and writing CSV files"}
#### Reading and writing CSV files
::: {.panel-tabset}
### R
```{r}
#| label: reading-R
#| code-fold: true
# Read a CSV file
data <- read.csv("data/example.csv")

# Inspect the first rows
head(data)

# Write to a CSV file
write.csv(data, "data/output.csv", row.names = FALSE)

```
### Python
```{python}
#| label: reading-py
#| code-fold: true
import pandas as pd

# Read a CSV file
data = pd.read_csv("data/example.csv")

# Inspect the first rows
print(data.head())

# Write to a CSV file
data.to_csv("data/output.csv", index=False)
```
:::
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Example: Reading Excel files"}
### Reading Excel files
::: {.panel-tabset}
### R
```{r}
#| label: reading-R-excel
#| code-fold: true
# Requires the 'readxl' package
library(readxl)

# Read an Excel file (first sheet by default)
data_xlsx <- read_excel("data/example.xlsx")

head(data_xlsx)

```
### Python
```{python}
#| label: reading-py-excel
#| code-fold: true
import pandas as pd

# Read an Excel file (first sheet by default)
data_xlsx = pd.read_excel("data/example.xlsx")

print(data_xlsx.head())
```
:::
:::

>**Tip:** Always check your working directory with `getwd()` in R or `os.getcwd()` in Python,  
>and adjust file paths accordingly so your scripts can locate the files without errors.


### Basic Plotting
Visualizing your data early helps detect patterns, trends, and anomalies before doing complex analysis.
Good visualizations tell a story that can be understood even without statistical training.

Once you have data loaded, visualization becomes a powerful tool to understand its structure and detect patterns at a glance.
In this section, we will cover simple plots using **base R** and **matplotlib** in Python.
The goal is to give you a minimal but functional starting point for plotting; we will explore more advanced visualization libraries in later chapters.

::: {.callout-note title="Example: Basic plotting in R & Python"}
#### Plotting numeric variables
::: {.panel-tabset}

### R
```{r}
# Read the CSV example file
data <- read.csv("data/example.csv")

# Basic scatter plot: Age vs Salary
plot(
  data$Age, data$Salary,
  main = "Age vs Salary",
  xlab = "Age",
  ylab = "Salary",
  col = "blue",
  pch = 19
)

# Basic barplot: Count by Department
dept_counts <- table(data$Department)
barplot(dept_counts,
        main = "Number of Employees by Department",
        col = "lightblue")
```
### Python
```{python}
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Read the CSV example file
data = pd.read_csv("data/example.csv")

# Basic scatter plot: Age vs Salary
plt.scatter(data["Age"], data["Salary"], color="blue")
plt.title("Age vs Salary")
plt.xlabel("Age")
plt.ylabel("Salary")
plt.show()

# Basic barplot: Count by Department
dept_counts = data["Department"].value_counts()
dept_counts.plot(kind="bar", color="lightblue")
plt.title("Number of Employees by Department")
plt.ylabel("Count")
plt.show()
```
:::
:::

>**Tip:** When creating plots, always label your axes and provide a clear title.  
>Good labeling makes your plots informative without requiring extra explanation.


### Basic Descriptive Statistics
Descriptive statistics provide a numerical summary of your data, highlighting key aspects like central tendency and variability.
They are the foundation for more advanced inferential methods and help validate assumptions about your dataset.

After loading and visualizing data, the next step is to summarize it numerically.
Descriptive statistics help you understand the central tendency, spread, and overall distribution of your variables.
In this section, we will compute common measures such as the **mean**, **median**, **minimum**, **maximum**, and **standard deviation**.

::: {.callout-note title="Example: Descriptive statistics in R & Python"}
#### Summary statistics
::: {.panel-tabset}

### R
```{r}
# Read the CSV example file
data <- read.csv("data/example.csv")

# Quick summary of all variables
summary(data)

# Mean, median, standard deviation of Salary
mean(data$Salary)
median(data$Salary)
sd(data$Salary)

# Minimum and maximum Age
min(data$Age)
max(data$Age)
```
### Python
```{python}
import pandas as pd

# Read the CSV example file
data = pd.read_csv("data/example.csv")

# Quick summary of all variables
print(data.describe())

# Mean, median, standard deviation of Salary
print(data["Salary"].mean())
print(data["Salary"].median())
print(data["Salary"].std())

# Minimum and maximum Age
print(data["Age"].min())
print(data["Age"].max())
```
:::
:::

>**Tip:** Use quick summary functions like summary() in R or .describe() in Python to get an instant overview of your dataset.

### Mini-Project: From Raw Data to Insight

In this mini-project you will practice a complete workflow:
1. Load a dataset.
2. Inspect and clean the data if necessary.
3. Calculate basic summaries.
4. Create a simple visualization.
5. Save the results.

We will use the file `data/example.csv` created earlier in this chapter.

#### Step 1 — Load and inspect the data
::: {.panel-tabset}

### R
```{r}
data <- read.csv("data/example.csv")

# Inspect structure and first rows
str(data)
head(data)
summary(data)
```

### Python
```{python}
import pandas as pd

data = pd.read_csv("data/example.csv")

# Inspect structure and first rows
print(data.info())
print(data.head())
print(data.describe())
```
:::

>**Tip:** Inspecting your dataset before any analysis helps identify missing values, incorrect types, and unexpected entries.

#### Step 2 — Summarize by department
We will calculate the number of employees, mean salary, and mean age for each department.

::: {.panel-tabset}

### R
```{r}
summary_tbl <- aggregate(
  cbind(Salary, Age) ~ Department,
  data = data,
  FUN = function(x) c(mean = mean(x), n = length(x))
)

# Extract and rename columns
summary_tbl$Mean_Salary <- summary_tbl$Salary[, "mean"]
summary_tbl$N <- summary_tbl$Salary[, "n"]
summary_tbl$Mean_Age <- summary_tbl$Age[, "mean"]

summary_tbl <- summary_tbl[, c("Department", "N", "Mean_Salary", "Mean_Age")]
summary_tbl
```

### Python
```{python}
summary_tbl = (
    data.groupby("Department")
        .agg(N=("Name", "count"),
             Mean_Salary=("Salary", "mean"),
             Mean_Age=("Age", "mean"))
        .reset_index()
)
print(summary_tbl)
```
:::

>**Tip:** Grouping and summarizing helps reveal patterns and differences between categories in your dataset.

#### Step 3 — Plot mean salary by department
::: {.panel-tabset}

### R
```{r}
barplot(
  summary_tbl$Mean_Salary,
  names.arg = summary_tbl$Department,
  main = "Mean Salary by Department",
  ylab = "Mean Salary",
  col = "lightblue"
)
```

### Python
```{python}
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

plt.bar(summary_tbl["Department"], summary_tbl["Mean_Salary"], color="lightblue")
plt.title("Mean Salary by Department")
plt.ylabel("Mean Salary")
plt.xlabel("Department")
plt.show()
```
:::

>**Tip:** Keep your plots simple and clear. Colors and labels should help the reader understand the data, not distract from it.

#### Step 4 — Save your results
::: {.panel-tabset}

### R
```{r}
write.csv(summary_tbl, "data/summary_by_department.csv", row.names = FALSE)
```

### Python
```{python}
summary_tbl.to_csv("data/summary_by_department.csv", index=False)
```
:::

>**Tip:** Saving intermediate results is useful when your analysis involves multiple steps or when you want to share summaries without the raw data.


## Exploring Quantitative Variables

Quantitative variables are numerical in nature and can be **discrete** (taking specific separated values) or **continuous** (capable of taking any value within a range).  
Understanding their distribution is essential for summarizing and comparing data.

### Grouping data into classes
When dealing with continuous variables, we often create **classes** or **intervals** to summarize the data.  
This involves deciding:

- The **number of classes** $k$
- The **width of each interval**
- Ensuring classes are **mutually exclusive** (no overlap) and **exhaustive** (cover all data points)

A widely used guideline is **Sturges’ rule**:

$$
k \approx 1 + 3.3 \cdot \log_{10}(n)
$$

Where $n$ is the number of observations.

The class width can be calculated as:

$$
\text{width} = \frac{\text{max} - \text{min}}{k}
$$

#### Example: Creating classes

Let’s use the `Salary` column from `data/example.csv` and group it into classes.

::: {.panel-tabset}
### R
```{r}
data <- read.csv("data/example.csv")

n <- nrow(data)
k <- ceiling(1 + 3.3 * log10(n)) # Sturges' rule
width <- ceiling((max(data$Salary) - min(data$Salary)) / k)

# Create intervals and frequency table
breaks <- seq(min(data$Salary), max(data$Salary) + width, by = width)
freq_table <- table(cut(data$Salary, breaks = breaks, right = FALSE))
freq_table
```
### Python
```{python}
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import math

data = pd.read_csv("data/example.csv")

n = len(data)
k = math.ceil(1 + 3.3 * math.log10(n)) # Sturges' rule
width = math.ceil((data["Salary"].max() - data["Salary"].min()) / k)

# Create intervals and frequency table
bins = np.arange(data["Salary"].min(), data["Salary"].max() + width, width)
freq_table = pd.cut(data["Salary"], bins=bins, right=False).value_counts().sort_index()
print(freq_table)
```
:::

>**Tip:** Rounding up the class width ensures all observations fit neatly into the intervals.

### Cumulative frequencies
The **cumulative absolute frequency** $N_j$ is the number of observations up to and including the $j$-th class.  
The **cumulative relative frequency** $F_j$ is $\frac{N_j}{n}$.

::: {.panel-tabset}
### R
```{r}
cum_abs <- cumsum(freq_table)
cum_rel <- cum_abs / n
data.frame(Class = names(freq_table),
           Freq = as.vector(freq_table),
           CumAbs = cum_abs,
           CumRel = cum_rel)
```

### Python
```{python}
cum_abs = freq_table.cumsum()
cum_rel = cum_abs / n
freq_df = pd.DataFrame({
    "Class": freq_table.index.astype(str),
    "Freq": freq_table.values,
    "CumAbs": cum_abs.values,
    "CumRel": cum_rel.values
})
print(freq_df)
```
:::

>**Tip:** Cumulative frequencies are useful for identifying percentiles and medians directly from grouped data.

### Visualizing continuous data

**Histogram**: Displays the distribution of a quantitative variable by showing frequencies for each class.

**Frequency polygon**: Connects the midpoints of histogram bars with straight lines.

**Ogive**: Plots the cumulative frequencies, useful for identifying medians and percentiles.

::: {.panel-tabset}
### R
```{r}
# Histogram
hist(data$Salary,
     breaks = breaks,
     right = FALSE,
     col = "lightblue",
     main = "Salary Distribution",
     xlab = "Salary")

# Frequency polygon
mids <- (breaks[-1] + breaks[-length(breaks)]) / 2
plot(mids, as.vector(freq_table), type = "o", col = "blue",
     main = "Frequency Polygon", xlab = "Salary", ylab = "Frequency")

# Ogive
plot(mids, cum_abs, type = "o", col = "red",
     main = "Ogive", xlab = "Salary", ylab = "Cumulative Frequency")
```
### Python
```{python}
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Histogram
plt.hist(data["Salary"], bins=bins, edgecolor="black", color="lightblue")
plt.title("Salary Distribution")
plt.xlabel("Salary")
plt.ylabel("Frequency")
plt.show()

# Frequency polygon
mids = (bins[:-1] + bins[1:]) / 2
plt.plot(mids, freq_table.values, marker="o", color="blue")
plt.title("Frequency Polygon")
plt.xlabel("Salary")
plt.ylabel("Frequency")
plt.show()

# Ogive
plt.plot(mids, cum_abs.values, marker="o", color="red")
plt.title("Ogive")
plt.xlabel("Salary")
plt.ylabel("Cumulative Frequency")
plt.show()
```
:::

>**Tip:** Use consistent class boundaries for all plots to ensure visual comparability.

### Practice

1. Group the `Age` variable into classes using Sturges’ rule and create the frequency table.  
2. Draw the histogram, frequency polygon, and ogive for `Age`.  
3. Identify the median salary from the ogive.
